How to use your command center

  1. Each class has its own tab — Principles · Manufacturing · InSPIRESS. Inside: a Present & print index (what's ready at a glance), the year arc (tap to open), and the built lesson plans, week by week.
  2. Present pops out into its own window — drag it to the projector, hit ⛶ Fullscreen. Space/→ next, ← back. First time, allow pop-ups.
  3. Print a day: 🖨 Print gives just that day's slides + worksheet, ready for Google Classroom.
  4. Syllabi: 📄 all three — half-sheet, print & cut.

ELPS key: CD clarify directions · ET extra time · PN peer/native-language support · PV pre-teach vocabulary · RS rephrase/repeat/slow down · VC visual cues · WT wait time · DP pictorial representation (ELPS 19 TAC §74.4).

Worksheet(s) - print as-is

Engineering Notebook - Setup, First Entry & Documentation Audit

Name: ______________________ Date: __________ Period: ______

A professional engineering notebook is a legal and technical record. Companies keep them bound, page-numbered, dated, and periodically witnessed so an entry can be trusted and reproduced months later - and can even settle a patent dispute. Today you set yours up to that standard and audit a sample against it.

Part A - Set up to standard (do now)

  1. Cover: full name, class, period, and school year on the front.
  2. Pages 1-3: reserve and title them "Table of Contents."
  3. Number every page (bottom outer corner) and date every entry.
  4. Permanent ink. Cross out mistakes with a single line - never erase, never tear out.
  5. Strike a diagonal line through any large blank space so nothing can be added later.
PageDateEntry title
1Notebook standards + first entry
2
3

Part B - Write a complete first entry

Use every field a professional would. Measure a small object at your table (phone, eraser, USB plug) with a ruler.

  1. Date & title:
  2. Purpose (what am I recording, and why?):
  3. Procedure (what I did, in order):
Labeled sketch of your object - name 3 parts and add 2 measured dimensions WITH units
  1. Data: length = ______ mm, width = ______ mm (write the unit every time)
  2. Result / next step:

Part C - Audit a flawed entry (analysis)

A classmate's entry reads: "Made the thing. It was about 8 long. Erased the part that was wrong. Looks good." There is no date, no units, and a page was torn out earlier.

  1. List four standard violations you can identify:
  2. Rewrite the measurement line correctly (add a unit + a tolerance, e.g. 8.0 ± 0.1 cm):

Part D - Record measurements like a pro (units & precision)

Raw readingRewrite it correctly (value + unit + tolerance)
74 (desk, cm ruler)
2.5 (bolt, mm caliper)
  1. A mm ruler can be trusted to about ±0.5 mm. Explain why writing "8.00000 mm" is dishonest about your precision:

Part E - Professional skills (scenario)

  1. Your test data looks worse than a teammate expected, and they ask you to "round it up so we look good." What is the engineering-integrity response, and why does it matter for safety?

Rubric self-score

StandardMax ptsYour score
Cover + TOC + numbered/dated pages4
Complete entry (all fields + labeled sketch)4
Measurements include units2
Total10

Engineering Fields, Careers & Technical Sketch

Name: ______________________ Date: __________ Period: ______

Part A - Guided viewing: What is engineering?

  1. In one sentence, how is engineering different from science (use the words "discover" and "design under constraints")?
  2. Name four engineering disciplines and, for one, a milestone from its history with an approximate era:
  3. Describe one real problem an engineer solved in the video and the constraint they had to respect:

Part B - Product to discipline: a systems breakdown

Pick ONE product: e-scooter, game console, or electric toothbrush. Break it into subsystems.

SubsystemDiscipline responsibleWhat it optimizes (the goal)

Part C - Careers & pathways

DisciplineA product they buildEducation pathApprox. median pay (US)
Civil
Mechanical
Software / Computer

Many engineering fields report median pay roughly $80k-$130k/yr. Give one reason employers pay engineers a premium:

Part D - Technical sketch (communicate a design)

Sketch one engineered object as an isometric (3D) OR three orthographic views. This is drafting, not art.

Annotated sketch: 3 labeled subsystems, 2 dimensions WITH units, 1 note, and a title block (name / date / scale)

Part E - Engineering argument

  1. "A software developer is really an engineer." Agree or disagree, and defend it using the definition design under constraints. Name one constraint a software engineer must satisfy.

Reflection: Which discipline best fits how YOU like to solve problems, and why?

Day 1 - Procedures, Lab Safety & Design Notebook

Aug 10
45-min agenda

ObjectiveStudents will classify manufacturing-lab hazards, apply the NIOSH hierarchy of controls to select the most effective control for a given task, complete a Job Safety Analysis (JSA) with a likelihood x severity risk score, and set up a dated, numbered engineering design notebook as a professional record.
TEKS§127.15(d)(1) CTE employability skills - safety, workplace expectations & teamwork
Emergent bilingual supportELPS/EB supports at grade level: hazard-class icons and a live tool demo (VC, DP); pre-teach hierarchy-of-controls terms with a labeled pyramid before use (PV); JSA drafted with a bilingual peer and sentence stems for the 'control + justification' cell (PN, CD); wait time and rephrase/slow on the risk-scoring steps (WT, RS); extra time to finish the notebook set-up (ET).
Design notebookSet up cover, table of contents, numbered/dated pages. First entry: one thing you want to design and build this year.

Worksheet(s) - print as-is

Job Safety Analysis (JSA) + Risk Scoring

Name: ________________________ Date: __________ Period: ______
A Job Safety Analysis breaks a task into steps, identifies the hazard in each step, scores the risk, and assigns the highest-level control that fits. Engineers do this before the work starts. Score Likelihood (L) and Severity (S) from 1 (low) to 5 (high); Risk = L x S.

Part A - Classify the hazard

Write the hazard class (Mechanical, Electrical, Thermal, Chemical, Ergonomic, or Noise) beside each situation.

Situation in the shopHazard class
Reaching across a spinning drill bit
Fumes while gluing ABS plastic
Frayed power cord on a belt sander
Lifting a 40 lb steel plate from the floor repeatedly
Touching stock just off the band saw blade

Part B - Job Safety Analysis for a real task

Chosen task (pick one: bench grinder, drill press, band saw, soldering iron, 3D printer):
For each step, name the hazard, score L and S, compute Risk = L x S, then give the strongest control that fits and its hierarchy level (Elimination / Substitution / Engineering / Administrative / PPE).

Task stepHazardLSRisk = LxSControl + hierarchy level
1. Set up________
2. Operate________
3. Operate________
4. Clean up________

Part C - Prioritize & justify

  1. Which step has the highest risk number?
  2. You may only add one new control before starting. Which step gets it, and why does the risk score justify that choice?
  3. One of your controls above is PPE. Explain why PPE alone is not enough and what stronger control backs it up.

Part D - Engineering judgment

A classmate says "we don't need a guard, we'll just be careful and wear gloves." Using the hierarchy of controls, explain in 2-3 sentences why an engineer rejects that plan.

Lab-Safety Agreement & Non-Negotiables

Name: ________________________ Date: __________ Period: ______

Part A - The non-negotiables (complete each rule)

  1. Two things I must check or do before operating any powered tool:
  2. If a tool is broken, a cord is frayed, or something spills, I will immediately:
  3. Before I clear a jam or service a machine, I will:
  4. Two pieces of PPE this shop requires and when each is used:
  5. One action that is never allowed near rotating equipment:

Part B - Near-miss reflection

Describe a "near-miss" you have seen (kitchen, garage, sports, shop) and the control that would have removed the hazard:

I have read the lab-safety rules, I understand the hierarchy of controls, and I agree to follow every posted procedure.
Student signature: ______________________ Date: __________

Worksheet(s) - print as-is

Production Systems Analysis: Inputs, Value-Added & Cost

Name: ________________________ Date: __________ Period: ______
Analyze how a product is manufactured as a system. Show all calculations with units.

Part A - The six inputs

Choose a real product (skateboard, water bottle, phone case, bike frame):
Identify a specific example of each input for that product.

InputSpecific example for your product
Materials
Machines / tools
Labor
Methods
Energy
Information / capital

Part B - Classify with justification

Name the production type (Job / Batch / Repetitive / Continuous) and justify using volume and variety.

ScenarioTypeJustification (volume + variety)
A machine shop makes 1 custom titanium bracket for a race team
A shop runs 800 identical steel brackets, then switches to a new part
A plant assembles 1,200 identical refrigerators per day on one line
A refinery produces gasoline nonstop, 24/7

Part C - Value-added ratio (calculate)

A part moves through the shop with the times below. Value-added (VA) steps are marked.

StepTime (min)VA or Waste?
Saw to length (VA)3VA
Wait for mill150Waste
Mill features (VA)9VA
Move to inspection20Waste
Wait in QC queue210Waste
Deburr & finish (VA)4VA
  1. Total value-added time = ____ min    Total lead time = ____ min
  2. Value-added ratio = VA / total = ________ = ______ % (show the division)
  3. To cut lead time, which step would you attack first, and why does the data point there (not at the machines)?

Part D - Unit cost & choosing a production type

Fixed (tooling + setup) = $3,000. Variable (material + labor) = $8 per unit. Unit cost = 8 + 3000/Q.

Quantity QUnit cost = 8 + 3000/Q
25 units$
150 units$
1,000 units$

A customer wants 30 units this year. Based on your unit-cost numbers, is a high-volume continuous line the right choice for this order? Justify with the cost trend.

Week 1
Monday

Day 1 - Procedures, Syllabus & Design Notebook

Aug 10
45-min agenda
6Bell-work: In your notebook, write one sentence on what separates *engineering* from *building*. We'll test it against the professional definition.
10The engineering design process: seven stages, and why documentation is 'stage zero'
10The language of a real problem: criteria vs. constraints, framed around the InSPIRESS payload challenge
13Build your design notebook to professional standard + write your first framed-problem entry
6Exit ticket: sort four statements into criteria/constraint and write one measurable success criterion
ObjectiveStudents will set up a professional engineering design notebook to documentation standards (numbered, dated, permanent, witness-ready), sequence the seven stages of the formal engineering design process, distinguish design criteria from constraints, and write a first notebook entry that frames a candidate InSPIRESS payload as a measurable design problem.
TEKS§127.406(d)(8)(A) maintain records of the engineering design process; 127.15(d)(2) employability skills
Emergent bilingual supportELPS/EB supports: pre-teach *criteria*, *constraint*, *iteration*, *specification* with a bilingual visual glossary and icons (PV, DP, VC); model the notebook setup live under the doc cam with numbered steps (CD, RS); provide sentence stems for the framed-problem entry — 'A successful design must ___, measured by ___ (units)'; 'A constraint I cannot violate is ___' (RS); pair EB students to talk through the criteria/constraint sort before writing (PN, WT); allow extra time on the notebook build (ET).
Design notebookSet it up today: cover, table of contents, numbered/dated pages. First entry = one thing you want to design or present this year.
Slide deck (30 slides) - Engineering Design & the Professional Notebook  ·  click ▶ Present for fullscreen
Worksheet(s) - print as-is

Design Notebook Standard + Define-Phase Problem Framing

Name: ______________________ Date: __________ Period: ______
A professional engineering notebook is a dated, numbered, permanent record. Complete every part in ink.

Part A — Notebook standard (self-audit)

  1. Cover shows your name, class, and year. (initial when done)
  2. Pages 1–3 reserved and ruled as a Table of Contents: # | Date | Topic | Page.
  3. Every page numbered; every entry dated; entries kept in date order.
  4. State the rule for a mistake (why you never erase):
  5. Why is an undocumented calculation treated, professionally, as work that never happened?

Part B — Criteria vs. constraints

Label each C = criterion (a dial we maximize / score) or X = constraint (a gate; pass/fail). Rewrite each vague item as measurable (value + unit).

#RequirementC or XRewrite as measurable (value + unit)
1Payload should be lightweight
2Must fit the 1U (10×10×10 cm) envelope
3Takes useful science images
4Uses no more than 2.0 W
5Should be reliable

Part C — Write a formal problem statement

Pick a payload idea. Frame it the way an engineer would.

  1. Problem in one sentence (name the stakeholder + the goal):

Three constraints (each: value + unit + how you would verify it):

ConstraintValue + unitHow you'll verify it
Mass
Power
Envelope / volume
  1. Three criteria to maximize (each measurable): a) b) c)

Part D — First iteration + reflection

  1. Write your first next step like an engineer: “Next, I will research ___ to answer ___.”
  2. Reflection: which is harder to write well — a criterion or a constraint? Why?

45-min agenda

7The unit of a technical argument: claim → evidence → interpretation

8Measurement uncertainty: precision vs. accuracy and how to report it
4Exit ticket
ObjectiveStudents will analyze technical communication using the claim–evidence–interpretation structure, apply significant-figure rules to measured quantities, convert and combine units by dimensional analysis with cancellation shown, and report a measured result with appropriate uncertainty.

Design notebookWrite the 3 presentation rules. Keep the unit-conversion example with all steps shown.

Technical Communication + Measurement: Evidence, Sig Figs, Units, Uncertainty

Name: ______________________ Date: __________ Period: ______
Show every unit and every step. A bare number earns no credit — engineers show the work.

Part A — Build the argument (claim → evidence → interpretation)

Use the data table to complete a technical argument. The power budget is 2.0 W.

Power-draw trial123Mean
Watts (W)1.551.621.60
  1. Mean draw (W), correct sig figs:
  2. Claim:
  3. Evidence (cite your number):
  4. Interpretation (pass/fail + margin as a %):

Part B — Significant figures

  1. Sig figs in each: 0.0300 ____ 1050 ____ 1050. ____ 2.00×10³ ____
  2. Round 88.94 mm to 2 s.f.:
  3. Compute with correct s.f.: 12.0 cm × 3.1 cm = (unit?)
  4. Compute with correct s.f.: 5.00 mm + 4.9 mm =

Part C — Dimensional analysis (show cancellation)

#ConvertSetup (show units cancel)Answer (s.f.)
16.0 in → mm
2100. mm → in
32.0 W over a 92-min orbit → J
45.0 MB/day → kB/hour

Part D — Uncertainty

A caliper reads to 0.1 mm. Three reads of a pin: 4.98, 5.02, 5.00 mm.

  1. Mean: Range:
  2. Report as value ± uncertainty (half the range):
  3. A scale reads 2.001, 2.000, 2.002 kg but the true mass is 2.500 kg. It is __________ (precise / accurate / both / neither). Explain:

Part E — Reflection

  1. Why does writing 89.0 mm claim more than writing 89 mm?

Tentative - wiggle days are built into every unit, so moving things around never breaks the plan.

The Engineering Design Notebook — your whole-year tool

Not just some pages — a system. One bound composition book each student keeps and uses every class day, all year: bellwork, notes, sketches, vocabulary, exit tickets, and project logs all live inside it. Graded on a rubric every two weeks, and it is how they study for their certification — same setup in both classes, so you run one routine.

Where vocabulary goes — and how

Back of the book (pp. 181–200). Four columns, English + Spanish, always with a sketch — consistent and review-ready for the certification:

Term (EN / ES)Meaning (my words)SketchSentence
prototype / prototipoa first model you build to test an idea✏️"We built a cardboard prototype first."
tolerance / toleranciahow much a size is allowed to be off✏️"The tolerance was ±1 mm."

Cognates (diseño, material, estructura, prototipo) are flagged so Spanish speakers get instant footholds.

Notebook check — 20 pts, every 2 weeks

Completeness — all class days present5
Dated entries (date + entry # + page)3
Table of Contents kept current3
Vocabulary (all 4 columns filled)4
Sketches present & labeled3
Neatness & pen/pencil convention2

Fast check (< 1 min/book): "open to entry #7, your best sketch, and today," then verify 2 random ToC lines. Stamp the glued-in rubric.

Day-1 setup (fits 45 minutes)

  1. Name on the cover and spine.
  2. Glue the Notebook Map + rubric to the inside cover.
  3. p.1 Title Page — Engineering Design Notebook · name · class · period · 2026–27.
  4. p.2 About the Engineer — finish the sentences + draw your logo.
  5. pp.3–6 Table of Contents — rule 4 columns: # | Date | Topic | Page.
  6. p.7 copy the 5 rules; p.8 glue the rubric + check log.
  7. Number pages 1–8; flip to the back, label p.177 Reference and p.181 Vocabulary Bank (rule the 4 vocab columns).
  8. Write your first ToC line: "Notebook Setup — p.1."

The 5 rules (a real engineer's record)

  1. Write in blue/black pen. Sketch in pencil.
  2. Date every entry.
  3. Mistakes: one line through + initials. Never scribble, white-out, or tear out a page.
  4. Number every page and add it to the Table of Contents.
  5. Neat enough that someone else could repeat your work.

Why: an engineer's notebook is a dated record of what you did and when — that is why you never tear out a page.

How to run it

  2. Each day: hit ▶ Present for that part, then they work the matching page.

  4. Friday: collect the whole packet. 20 points per part, 100 total.
